stem:
A 29-year-old woman develops demyelination of central axons, and her nerve conduction studies show slowed signal propagation.

In a healthy myelinated axon, propagation is fast because the action potential travels by which of the following mechanisms?

options.label: A
options.text: Glial cells actively propelling the depolarization down the fiber
options.misconception: A passive insulating sheath is being given an active transport role.
options.explanation: Schwann cells and oligodendrocytes only wrap and insulate the axon; the signal still propagates by voltage-gated Na+ channel opening, concentrated at the nodes.

options.label: B
options.text: Opening voltage-gated channels continuously along the entire membrane
options.misconception: The slower unmyelinated strategy is being ascribed to myelinated fibers.
options.explanation: Continuous conduction, with channels opening along the whole membrane, characterizes unmyelinated axons and is slower; myelinated segments regenerate the signal only at nodes.

options.label: C
options.text: Widening the axon so that internal resistance to ion flow falls
options.misconception: A separate, size-based determinant of speed is being substituted for the myelin mechanism.
options.explanation: Larger diameter does speed conduction by lowering resistance, but that applies to any axon; the specific advantage of myelination is saltatory, node-to-node propagation.

options.label: D
options.text: Regenerating only at the nodes of Ranvier, leaping from node to node
options.misconception: None; myelinated fibers conduct saltatorily between exposed nodes.
options.explanation: Voltage-gated Na+ channels cluster at the nodes of Ranvier; the depolarization spreads passively under the myelin and is renewed at each node, so the signal effectively jumps node to node and is much faster than continuous conduction.

options.label: E
options.text: Amplifying the voltage at each segment so the signal grows larger
options.misconception: The all-or-none signal is being treated as size-adjustable.
options.explanation: Action potentials are all-or-none and always peak near the same voltage; nodes renew the depolarization to the same amplitude rather than amplifying it.

context: Learning objective: explain saltatory conduction. In myelinated axons, voltage-gated Na+ channels exist only at the nodes of Ranvier, so the action potential jumps node to node and travels faster than continuous conduction.
imageCaption: Neuron RMP, threshold AP, refractory period, saltatory conduction, EPSP/IPSP summation.
